title: Alcohol use: recognising harm and getting support safely
intro: Alcohol-related problems are not defined only by a single drink count. Difficulty controlling drinking, repeated harm and withdrawal symptoms can all matter. Alcohol can affect physical health, mood, sleep, relationships and safety. Support is available without waiting for a crisis. If your body has become dependent, stopping suddenly can be dangerous, so getting help includes planning a safe change rather than attempting an unsupported detox.

sections.heading: Describe the pattern without judging yourself
paragraphs: Useful signs include drinking more than intended, unsuccessful attempts to cut down, craving and continuing despite problems. Needing increasing amounts or drinking to relieve shaking may suggest dependence. Record what you usually drink, including container sizes, stronger drinks and alcohol-free days. Different countries define a standard drink differently, so describe the actual beverage and amount rather than relying on a unit label alone. This information supports an assessment; it is not a moral test.

sections.heading: Recognise when stopping needs medical help
paragraphs: Shaking, sweating, nausea, anxiety or a racing heartbeat after reducing alcohol can be withdrawal. People with previous severe withdrawal, seizures or major health problems need particular caution. Do not use an online schedule or someone else's sedatives to manage withdrawal yourself. Contact a clinician or addiction service before an abrupt stop if dependence is possible. Confusion, hallucinations, a seizure or severe agitation during withdrawal require emergency help.

sections.heading: Ask for a complete health assessment
paragraphs: A consultation can explore drinking, medicines, nutrition, liver health, mental health and immediate safety. Be clear about other substances and whether you are pregnant or might be. Blood tests may help identify health effects, but a normal result does not prove that drinking is harmless. Care may involve primary care, specialist addiction services or hospital treatment, depending on withdrawal risk and other needs. Explain practical barriers such as work, childcare, money or privacy concerns.

sections.heading: Build support beyond withdrawal management
paragraphs: A longer-term plan may include psychological treatment, medicines selected by a clinician, peer support and help with sleep or social difficulties. Withdrawal treatment alone does not address every reason for drinking. Discuss goals and what to do after a lapse without treating it as proof that recovery is impossible. Family members can offer support while setting boundaries, but should not take responsibility for supervising a potentially dangerous home detox.

sections.heading: Respond to intoxication and other immediate dangers
paragraphs: An unconscious person, someone difficult to wake, slow or irregular breathing, seizures or collapse after drinking needs emergency help. Do not assume they can simply sleep it off, and do not give more alcohol or try to sober them with coffee or a cold shower. Stay with them, monitor breathing and follow emergency instructions. Alcohol also affects driving and safe use of medicines; arrange a safe alternative rather than guessing when it has worn off.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: asking for a safe stopping plan
examples.text: Someone notices shaking before their first drink and wants to stop. They tell a clinician about this and about earlier attempts to cut down. They ask whether supervised withdrawal is needed instead of suddenly stopping alone or borrowing sleeping tablets.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: planning support after a lapse
examples.text: A person drinks again after a period of change. They contact their support service to discuss what happened and revise the plan. They describe any withdrawal symptoms and immediate risks, rather than assuming the lapse means treatment has failed or that another unsupported detox is safe.

questions: Do my symptoms suggest dependence or a risk of withdrawal?
What kind of support and medical monitoring would make change safer for me?
